Allen Gardiner
AL-un GARD-nur
proper noun
Allen, a name of Celtic origin commonly taken as “little rock” or “harmony”; Gardiner an English occupational surname, “keeper of a garden”; he sowed a seed in death that others reaped in life.

Biblical Definition

Allen Francis Gardiner (1794–1851) was an English naval officer who forsook the sea to become a missionary to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, and who died of starvation upon that desolate coast, his journals afterward kindling the mission he had longed to plant. A captain of distinction, he was converted to a deep and earnest faith and resolved to carry the gospel to the most neglected peoples of the earth. Turned back from one field after another — among the Zulus, in South America, among scattered tribes — he was never discouraged from the cause, holding that “while God gives me strength, failure will not daunt me.” At last he set out with six companions for the southern tip of the New World to reach the Yaghan people. Want of supplies, fierce weather, and the failure of a relief ship left the little band to perish one by one of hunger and cold; Gardiner himself died last, his diary recording praise to God to the very end. When the relief came too late and his words were read, the churches were so moved by his patient faith that the Patagonian (later South American) Missionary Society was strengthened and the work went forward, until the gospel took root among the very people he died to reach. He held the Great Commission a debt to every tribe, and proved that even a mission that seems to fail may, in the providence of God, become a seed (Joh 12:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

An English naval captain turned missionary to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego who starved to death on that coast, his journals fueling the mission afterward.

ALLEN GARDINER, an English naval officer and missionary (1794–1851) to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego.

He left a distinguished navy career to carry the gospel to the most neglected peoples of the earth.

Turned back from field after field, he held that failure would not daunt him while God gave him strength.

He and six companions perished of starvation and cold near the southern tip of South America.

His journals of patient faith stirred the church to take up the mission he died to begin (Joh 12:24).

Key Scripture

Joh 12:24 — "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."

Rev 2:10 — "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

Psa 23:4 — "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Modern Corruption

Gardiner’s costly venture is read by the modern mind as a foolish or even arrogant intrusion, missing the seed his death became.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chief distortion of Gardiner’s memory is not a culture-war revision but the worldly verdict that his death was mere folly — a man and his friends starving uselessly at the end of the earth. The Scripture judges otherwise. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit (Joh 12:24). What seemed a wasted life became the very seed of the South American mission, for his journals so moved the church that the work went forward until the Yaghan heard the gospel. The world counts such sacrifice loss; faith counts it sowing.

The lesson to recover is that the measure of a life is not visible success but faithfulness unto death (Rev 2:10). Gardiner died as those of Hebrews eleven died, not having received the promise but having seen it afar off, a stranger and pilgrim on the earth. His patient praise from the valley of the shadow rebukes a generation that abandons every labor that does not quickly prosper. The God who buried this seed in the cold soil of Tierra del Fuego raised from it a harvest, and so He often does with the costliest obedience.

Hebrew Roots

A gardener by name, he buried himself as a seed in barren soil, and God raised a harvest from his grave.

expand to see more

Gardiner — English occupational surname, “keeper of a garden,” a sower of seed.

Allen — a name of Celtic origin, often glossed “little rock” or “harmony.”

The figure that crowns his story is the buried corn of wheat that brings forth fruit (Joh 12:24).

“Patagonia” named the bleak southern land he gave his life to reach.

“Journal” from the Latin diurnalis, daily; his daily diary outlived and outlabored him.

Usage

"Allen Gardiner left the navy to carry the gospel to the forgotten peoples at the end of the earth."

"Though field after field was closed to him, Allen Gardiner refused to be daunted while God gave him strength."

"The dying words Allen Gardiner wrote in his journal moved the church to finish the work he had begun."
